routes.description: Establish bodily resurrection as the unifying historical explanation of the appearance testimony, early proclamation, witness conduct, and missing-body evidence.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the cited evidence supports a bodily postmortem event and the resurrection explains the combined evidence with fewer added assumptions than its rivals.

motionBridge.description: The cumulative historical evidence must make Jesus's bodily resurrection a reasonable conclusion.

centralBridges.description: The reported appearances must support encounters with the embodied risen Jesus rather than merely disembodied or private visions.
The early witnesses and converts must be sufficiently sincere and historically connected to the proclamation for their conduct to require explanation.
A historically credible burial and missing body must support resurrection over relocation, theft, or literary invention.
The resurrection hypothesis must account for the combined evidence more economically than a conjunction of naturalistic alternatives.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Rival miracle traditions must either be evidentially distinguishable or compatible with evaluating the Christian claims on their own evidence.
Pauline, Lukan, and Gospel traditions must preserve historically useful information despite their theological purposes.

routes.description: Show that the surviving testimony is too indirect, physically ambiguous, and comparably explainable by visionary, literary, or natural historical alternatives.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the record does not securely establish firsthand bodily encounters and the principal facts remain compatible with more ordinary rival explanations.

motionBridge.description: The available historical record must fail to warrant the specific conclusion that Jesus physically rose from death.

centralBridges.description: The appearance traditions must remain compatible with visionary experiences rather than encounters with an ordinary physical body.
The record must lack sufficiently direct and independent testimony to the claimed bodily appearances.
Comparable religious testimony must weaken any inference from sincerity, group reports, or persecution to supernatural truth.
Burial uncertainty, relocation, theft, or narrative construction must remain plausible explanations of the empty-tomb tradition.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Persecution evidence must not establish that eyewitnesses suffered specifically for affirming a witnessed bodily resurrection.
Differences and developing detail among the narratives must limit their use as straightforward historical corroboration.

sectionSelections.title: Physical or visionary appearances
sectionSelections.rationale: The motion specifically concerns physical resurrection, so the meaning of Pauline and Gospel appearance traditions is indispensable to both routes.

proSelections.proposition: Group appearances reported by Paul and Luke provide historical grounds for concluding that Jesus was alive after his death.
Paul taught embodied resurrection rather than disembodied survival, and the physical features of Jesus's appearances distinguish them from acknowledged visions.

conSelections.proposition: Christian apparition reports do little to establish resurrection because comparable experiences occur elsewhere and the sources are unclear about whether Jesus's risen body was physical.
Paul is unclear about a physical resurrection, while later Gospel appearance narratives become more elaborate and theological rather than supplying secure eyewitness history.

sectionSelections.title: Historical access to appearance testimony
sectionSelections.rationale: The evidential force of reported appearances depends on whether the surviving sources provide reliable and sufficiently independent access to the underlying claims.

proSelections.proposition: Luke is historically reliable and close to Paul, while Paul's encounter was comparable to apostolic appearances and the bounded appearance tradition resists a hallucination hypothesis.

conSelections.proposition: Evidence for Jesus before crucifixion is substantially stronger than evidence for postmortem appearances because the latter lacks independent extra-Christian corroboration.

sectionSelections.title: Rival miracle and witness claims
sectionSelections.rationale: Comparisons with other religious movements test whether group testimony, prior expectations, incentives, and persistence reliably discriminate the resurrection claim from rivals.

proSelections.proposition: Mormon miracle and witness claims are materially weaker analogues because natural incentives, prior expectations, source discrepancies, and contrary historical evidence reduce their credibility.

conSelections.proposition: Mormon witness and transfiguration traditions are at least comparable to early Christian appearance testimony, exposing how little can be verified about Paul's five-hundred-person report.
The alleged expectation and financial-interest differences between Mormon and Christian witnesses are unstable because Jesus predicted resurrection and Mary Magdalene supported his ministry.

sectionSelections.title: Sincerity, persecution, and martyrdom
sectionSelections.rationale: Costly commitment bears on witness sincerity only insofar as the historical record connects particular people, knowledge, and suffering to the resurrection proclamation.

proSelections.proposition: Apostolic suffering matters as evidence of sincere testimony by people positioned to know, and Christianity has additional explanatory features absent from the Mormon parallel.

conSelections.proposition: Persecution and movement growth do not distinguish early Christianity from Mormonism, while the historical basis for claiming that apostles accepted death for resurrection belief is sparse.
Persecution and martyrdom do not establish eyewitness knowledge of a bodily resurrection because the clearest early cases concern visionary experiences or unspecified beliefs.

sectionSelections.title: Burial, empty tomb, and alternatives
sectionSelections.rationale: A missing body provides a distinct route toward bodily resurrection only if the tomb tradition is historical and ordinary removal hypotheses fit the evidence less well.

proSelections.proposition: Apologetic purposes do not make a narrative false, and Matthew's dispute over a stolen body may preserve evidence that Jesus's body was genuinely missing.
Non-resurrection is only an umbrella for multiple specific hypotheses whose conjunction reduces probability, and grave robbery poorly fits the retained burial goods and known practices.

conSelections.proposition: Women discovering the tomb is narratively expected rather than an embarrassment criterion, while their immediate recourse to men and conflicting sequences weaken the apologetic inference.
An empty tomb, if there was one, is plausibly explained by temporary emergency burial followed by relocation or theft, neither of which requires resurrection.
